viz_reviews.summary: Reads as a pyramid instantly: three filled trapezoid tiers in slot colour, one apex, a rank of key lines, a wider base, each key line directly above its own supports. Hiding derived in tbpn empties the apex triangle (the synthesis that was never said); in classic it collapses the structure around a fact apex attached to nothing. Idea-bearing slot unmissable. Stats match graph.json in every state, build reproduces index.html byte-for-byte, consoles empty, 0 overlaps / 0 off-screen / 0 under cards on both examples.

notes: Research (recall): Barbara Minto, McKinsey's first female MBA hire (1963), developed the method to teach consultants to write; The Pyramid Principle (in-house 1978, Pitman 1987; later The Minto Pyramid Principle: Logic in Writing, Thinking and Problem Solving, 1996/2009). Object: a piece of reasoning meant for a reader, arranged answer-first. Slots: governing thought (the single sentence that answers the reader's question and sits at the apex), key lines (the pillars; each answers the question the governing thought raises in the reader's mind: Why? How? How do you know?; together the set must be MECE, mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive, a term Minto coined; a set is either a deductive chain, premise, premise, therefore, or an inductive group of the same kind of idea under one plural noun such as reasons, steps, problems, ordered by time, structure or degree), supports (the data, quotes and observations under each pillar; the base of the pyramid). Three rules: ideas at any level summarise the ideas grouped below them; ideas in a grouping are the same kind of idea; ideas in a grouping are in logical order. Vertical logic is a question-and-answer dialogue with the reader; horizontal logic is deductive or inductive. Justification: Miller's seven-plus-or-minus-two; the reader's mind groups whatever it receives, so the writer should impose the grouping first. The introduction uses SCQ (Situation, Complication, Question), filed in this library under minto-scqa; the pyramid proper starts at the Answer. Textbook use: Minto's opening illustration, a secretary's phone message about rescheduling a meeting told in the order the calls came in, against its pyramid form (reschedule, because it suits the attendees and the room is free); and the consultant's recommendation memo with three pillars. Common misuse: bottom-up narration (the story of the analysis before the answer); topic headings instead of assertions ('Costs' rather than 'Costs are rising'); intellectually blank summaries ('there are three problems') that group without synthesising; overlapping or incomplete key lines (not MECE); mixing deductive and inductive in one group; more than about five key lines; a governing thought that does not answer the question the reader has. Provenance expectation: supports are stated (fact); key lines are stated when the speaker enumerates ('three reasons') and derived when the speaker narrates bottom-up and the summary must be written; the governing thought is usually derived because speakers rarely state their one-sentence answer first, and when a speaker does state it, the stated sentence is a fact node and the synthesis the pyramid requires is a derived node above it. Scout: three candidates returned: (1) Elad Gil's three-pillar case on why the AI market is mis-sized, 2025-10-10, L3116-L3210; (2) Sean Henry (Stord) 'our three pillars are really a network, software and scale', 2025-05-16; (3) a host reading the WSJ 'why there will never be another Warren Buffett' piece (the person, the period, the package), 2025-05-05. Chose (1). Reason: it is the interesting provenance case rather than the tidiest pyramid. The speaker enumerates his pillars ('the first thing... a second thing... the third thing'), so the key lines and their group membership are facts with quoted ordinal connectives, but he puts an intellectually blank label on top ('two or three things that are underappreciated') and reaches his conclusion only after the pillars, so the governing thought - the synthesis Minto requires - has to be written. (2) was the closest to a textbook answer-first pyramid but is a founder's pitch in which every level is stated, so almost nothing would be derived; (3) is a host reading someone else's argument aloud, which makes the speaker attribution fuzzy. Candidate (2) is recorded here as the better example if a later reviewer wants an all-fact pyramid. Graph: classic = Minto's rescheduling note written as an original scenario text (11 nodes, 7 fact / 4 derived, 18 edges of which 2 are fact); tbpn = Elad Gil's three pillars (21 nodes, 17 fact / 4 derived, 30 edges of which 8 are fact). validate.mjs: 0 errors, 0 warnings. Design decision, deliberate and asymmetric: the two examples sit at opposite ends of the provenance range and are meant to be read together. In the classic, a bottom-up note, every statement is a fact and almost every edge is derived, so the facts-only view is a heap of statements with two local 'because' chains and an apex attached to nothing - which is exactly Minto's complaint about narrated messages. In the TBPN example the speaker enumerates, so pillar membership is carried by quoted ordinal connectives (fact edges fe1-fe3) and the derived work concentrates at the apex and on the fourth pillar. Second decision: the governing_thought slot holds three nodes - the derived synthesis (gt), the speaker's late conclusion (gt_stated, fact) and his blank grouping label (gt_group, fact) - applying SPEC 3's split rule to a slot that is partly stated and partly inferred. Third: idea_bearing_slot = governing_thought, because in this framework the opportunity is the synthesis nobody wrote; a second idea sits on the derived key line k4, which SPEC 3 allows ('normally only in the idea-bearing slot'). Entity spelling note: the node s11 uses 'Ripling' because that is how tbpn-transcripts/extractions/2025-10-10.json spells Rippling, and entities are the merge key.
